contributions.summary: Uses a model-I/model-II/model-III Summary ladder and explicitly lets Model I's upper-bound result trigger Model II.
Moves from Juneau wealth and glacier/crowding pressure to failed TBMP measures and the TSMP task.
Makes method selection visible through literature comparison and a numbered Our Work contract.
States that the supplied material lacks required data, then identifies and visualizes the needed inputs.
Excludes pandemic years and outliers before fitting, leaving a visible human modeling choice.
Admits missing tourist-income data and reduces the elasticity model rather than hiding the gap.
Discards two Pareto groups for concrete economic/environmental reasons before retaining the third.
Lets selected upper-bound variables trigger a new expenditure-feedback model.
Splits feedback into sufficient- and insufficient-revenue branches.
Reads heatmap coefficients into variable-specific policy actions.

A judge may value explicit data collection while challenging source traceability.

language_observations.summary: The Summary gives each model its own purpose-method-result paragraph and preserves body order.
A computed Model I result, not a generic transition, triggers Model II.
The Introduction uses a real conflict and failed existing policy before introducing the new plan.
Our Work repeats model nouns and numbered actions, making the later structure predictable.
Assumptions use premise-justification pairs with blunt repeated labels.
Data preparation admits that supplied material does not directly offer required inputs.
The fit section openly excludes pandemic years and outliers to stabilize estimation.
The source openly drops income after stating the missing-data condition.
The result section narrates why two candidate groups fail instead of reporting only a winner.
Upper-bound proximity creates a natural handoff to expenditure planning.
Feedback prose is organized by business condition: enough prior revenue versus not enough.
Sensitivity prose reads coefficient magnitude and then names a policy implication.
Transfer starts with local differences, then changes variables and refits functions.
Low-tourist transfer reverses actions rather than repeating Juneau recommendations.
Evaluation uses visibly separate strengths and weaknesses.
The memo uses audience, situation, model recap, numbered recommendations, limitation, and monitoring close.

models.summary: Map Juneau's wealth, crowding, glacier, resident, policy, transfer, and communication pressures into a three-model TSMP workflow.
Freeze market and preference premises, type decision variables, and collect Juneau data that the prompt does not directly provide.
Balance fiscal revenue, environmental damage, and resident satisfaction under policy and capacity constraints.
Combine three attraction receipts, visitor-fee increases, hotel spending, and hotel-tax changes.
Fit temperature and carbon footprint to visitor volume and minimize their normalized weighted combination.
Combine resident income benefit, road congestion, and infrastructure/waste pressure into a satisfaction score.
Bind attraction-specific visitor counts to total tourists before the demand model is introduced.
Relate tourist demand to income, price, and road area, remove unavailable income, insert fee and tax controls, and then impose temperature, carbon, and urban-capacity thresholds.
Generate a Pareto set across fiscal, environmental, and resident objectives under the feasible set.
Compare three distinct objective groups, discard environmental-harm and low-revenue groups, and retain four similar group-three candidates.
Use upper-bound road/capacity results to trigger a model allocating additional fee/tax revenue to S and G.
Update resident satisfaction differently when prior-year additional revenue can or cannot cover current expenditure.
Vary one decision variable by plus/minus ten percent with others fixed and inspect objective correlations.
Adapt the Juneau structure to Maldives attractions, spending, hotel tax, temperature, carbon, waste, and resident dependence.
Reverse policy priorities for low-tourist destinations, separate strengths/weaknesses, and translate Juneau outputs into a council memo.

results_trace.summary: The Summary reports a roughly 1.43-million next-year tourist scale, fee/tax changes, expenditure feedback, sensitivity, and transfer.
Groups 1 and 2 are discarded and four similar group-three solutions are retained.
The four listed solutions use x_0 around 1.3864-1.4836 and fee increases around 72.29-72.90 in source scale.
Road area and infrastructure capacity are used to motivate additional-revenue allocation.
Heatmap readings identify tourist restriction, fee/tax controls, road area, and infrastructure as influential.
Maldives equations and result chart generate a transferred candidate/sensitivity set.
Low-tourist destinations receive lower-price, attraction, and promotion recommendations.
The memo restates a TSMP package but leaves scale and implementation conflicts.

section_map.summary: Summary spans pages 1-1 and turns Juneau's wealth-pressure conflict, three models, objectives, NSGA-II, Pareto choice, expenditure feedback, sensitivity, Maldives transfer, and low-tourist use into a first-page decision ladder with an explicit model-I-to-II trigger before handing off to Introduction.

Introduction spans pages 3-4 and turns wilderness, cruise wealth, resident crowding, glacier retreat, TBMP limits, TSMP demand, official tasks, literature, and Our Work into a bounded problem contract and workflow before handing off to Assumptions.

Assumptions spans pages 5-6 and turns market stability, tourist preferences, scenic allocation, hotel choice, and additional local premises into a premise-consequence envelope before handing off to Notation.

Notation spans pages 6-6 and turns tourists, attractions, fees, hotel tax, road area, infrastructure, residents, waste, environment, and objectives into a variable and unit interface before handing off to Model Preparation.

Model Preparation spans pages 7-7 and turns data needs, database sites, Juneau map, tourist scale, temperature, carbon, roads, capacity, prices, and waste into a prepared Juneau input ledger before handing off to Multi-objective overview.

Multi-objective Overview spans pages 8-8 and turns fiscal revenue, environmental damage, resident satisfaction, direct controls, and capacity constraints into a multi-objective architecture contract before handing off to Fiscal Revenue.
Fiscal Revenue spans pages 9-10 and turns three attraction counts and fees, hotel occupancy/spending, tax rate, and policy increases into Equations (1)-(3) before handing off to Environmental Damage.

Environmental Damage spans pages 10-11 and turns visitor volume, temperature, carbon footprint, pandemic-year exclusion, historical extrema, and weights into Equations (4)-(6) before handing off to Resident Satisfaction.

Resident Satisfaction spans pages 11-13 and turns resident income, road congestion, infrastructure pressure, AHP weights, 2023 attitudes, road area, waste capacity, and population into Equations (7)-(8) and a weighted satisfaction interface before handing off to Constraints and demand.

Constraints and Demand Elasticity spans pages 13-15 and turns attraction closure, tourist limits, fee and tax increases, income, prices, road area, alternative-city spending, and environmental thresholds into Equations (9)-(18) before handing off to NSGA-II.

NSGA-II and Pareto Selection spans pages 16-17 and turns three objectives, feasible population, nondominated sorting, variation, 255 candidates, three distinct groups, and four similar solutions into a candidate set and an explicit exclude-retain chain before handing off to Expenditure feedback.

Expenditure Feedback spans pages 17-18 and turns upper-bound road/capacity variables, additional tax/fee revenue, expenditure costs, satisfaction weights, and prior-year revenue into Equations (19)-(22) and two expenditure branches before handing off to Sensitivity.

Sensitivity spans pages 18-19 and turns plus/minus ten-percent local perturbations, decision variables, three objectives, and a correlation heatmap into a heatmap-to-policy reading before handing off to Maldives Expansion.

Maldives Expansion spans pages 20-22 and turns Maldives attraction geography, tourists, emissions, temperature, prices, hotel occupancy, waste, residents, objectives, and result charts into Equations (23)-(25), transferred Pareto results, and a Juneau comparison before handing off to Low-tourist transfer.

Low-tourist Transfer spans pages 22-22 and turns low visitor volume, price sensitivity, promotion, welfare, project development, and tourist diversion into a qualitative low-tourism policy sketch before handing off to Evaluation.

Evaluation spans pages 23-23 and turns claimed comprehensiveness, quantification, practicality, stability, scalability, data limits, and proposed penalties into a source-authored strengths/weaknesses ledger before handing off to Memo.

Memo spans pages 24-24 and turns council audience, selected tourist volume, fee/tax changes, road/capacity spending, implementation recommendations, limits, and monitoring into a council-facing TSMP memo before handing off to References boundary.

Plan expenditure of additional revenue and connect it to sustainability.
Perform sensitivity analysis on important controls.
Adapt the model to another crowded destination and to low-tourist destinations.

unresolved_questions.summary: Contents, reference entries, running headers, MATHmodels watermarks, QR material, and third-party visual text are excluded from positive author-language evidence.
The opening glacier comparison is a visual source claim; its image provenance and quantitative series are not reproduced as a machine-readable data table.
The paper says existing TBMP measures are short-sighted and one-sided, but it does not define a measurable baseline against which TSMP improves trust or resident welfare.
NSGA-II is selected from a literature framework, but the paper provides no common benchmark or reproducible comparison with the alternatives it names.
The Our Work list promises a one-page memo and model generality while data, optimization settings, and implementation evidence remain incomplete.
Assumption 1 is explained twice with overlapping market-stability language, suggesting the premise ledger was not edited into one auditable statement.
Stable market structure and spending preferences remove demand shifts that the later elasticity and transfer sections treat as policy-sensitive.
Table 1 gives symbols but does not close units, time bases, bounds, or provenance for x_i, S, G, P_j, t_i, Delta t, r, and Delta r.
The data/database table lists websites but does not bind each numerical input to retrieval date, unit, transformation, or a frozen file hash.
The Juneau map supplies context but no coordinate-linked variable or spatial aggregation enters the equations.
Fiscal revenue, environmental damage, and resident satisfaction are placed in a multi-objective model without a published common scaling, weight, or Pareto preference rule.
The daily-tourist capacity and stable infrastructure premises are asserted before a carrying-capacity estimate or measurement protocol is shown.
The attraction-revenue equation prints x_0 before Delta t_i although the summation is indexed by i; the paper does not state whether the fee increase is per-attraction or total.
The revenue sum is written for three attractions, but the attraction list and x_i domain are not fully connected to the data table.
Equation (2) multiplies visitors, accommodation spending, and a tax-rate change without stating whether k and x_0 are daily, annual, or taxable occupied-room quantities.
Equation (3) repeats the x_0 Delta t_i indexing ambiguity and calls the combined expression a maximum without a stated decision domain or optimization operation.
Equation (4) is fitted after excluding pandemic years and outliers, but no observations, residuals, fit criterion, uncertainty, or competing functional form is published.
The prose calls the carbon relation exponential while Equation (5) is quadratic; no correction or model-selection evidence resolves the mismatch.
Equation (6) divides by historical minima and asserts weights 0.7 and 0.3, but it does not justify scale comparability, sign direction, or sensitivity to the weights.
The AHP comparison matrix appears to reuse a small resident survey/correlation basis as pairwise importance without reporting consistency ratio, respondent aggregation, or judgment uncertainty.
The 0.50/0.34/0.16 weights are interpreted as resident-income, congestion, and infrastructure pressure importance, but the bridge from the source matrix to policy utility is not calibrated.
The 2023 resident-attitude percentages are turned into a baseline score without a disclosed aggregation rule, denominator audit, or uncertainty.
Resident satisfaction combines income, road area, and waste-pressure ratios with weights, but the 2,800,000 conversion and each denominator's unit are unexplained.
The simplified satisfaction expression changes the visible scaling and omits an explicit mapping from the AHP weights to the displayed coefficients.
Equation (9) permits x_1+x_2+x_3 below x_0, then Equation (10) imposes equality by assumption; the lost slack is not tested as a feasible alternative.
The prose refers to earlier equations with inconsistent numbers, including calling the restriction and equality conditions (4) and (5), which weakens replay.
Equation (11) is introduced from an external demand-elasticity model, but the Juneau coefficient fit and tourist-income data are not available.
The paper omits the income term because tourist income data are unavailable, but does not quantify the resulting bias or compare a proxy-based specification.
Equation (12) uses 262.5 dollars from alternative cities while Equation (15) uses 243 dollars for Juneau; the switching rule is not stated.
The printed relation beta_2 = beta_3 = 100 conflicts with surrounding ratio prose and the derived -0.72 coefficient; the source is retained as ambiguous.
Equation (14) and (15) omit a visible derivation from beta ratios to -0.72 and do not report demand-response uncertainty.
Temperature and carbon constraints use midpoints of historical extremes without a policy, ecological, or statistical justification.
Equation (18) uses 2,800,000 tourist units, waste per tourist, and G in a ratio constrained below one, but the time basis and dimensional conversion are not closed.
The paper alternates between NSGA-II and NGSA-II, including the algorithm figure label; the implementation identity is therefore not fixed by the prose.
No population size, generation budget, crossover/mutation settings, random seed, feasibility repair, stopping rule, convergence trace, or code is supplied.
The paper reports 255 Pareto solutions and then reasons from groups, but gives no machine-readable candidate set, objective normalization, or selection rule.
Group 1 is excluded for environmental harm and group 2 for low revenue/satisfaction, yet the retained group-3 choice is not tied to an explicit preference or threshold rule.
Table 5 lists four similar solutions without identifying one selected row, tie-break criterion, uncertainty, or feasibility residual.
Additional revenue is modeled as x_0 times a fee increase plus hotel-tax increase, but the units and relation to Equation (3)'s attraction terms are not reconciled.
Decision variables and table values use x_i and x_0 as daily visitors, while the memo describes about 1.43 million next year without an explicit annual conversion.
S and G are described as upper-bound-active, then treated as importance evidence; an active bound does not by itself establish causal priority.
The expenditure equation introduces a_1 and a_2 but never supplies values, units, calibration, or budget feasibility.
Equations (21) and (22) split on prior revenue versus current cost but do not define equality handling, timing, caps, infeasible states, or a reproducible branch algorithm.
The ratio 6.5 is inferred from correlation coefficients rather than a cost-effectiveness or budget estimate; the correlation-to-cost mapping is unsupported.
The local perturbation heatmap is described as correlation strength, not a derivative or causal elasticity, and the perturbation grid and recalculation protocol are not published.
Claims that daily tourist limits dominate fixed fees or that hotel tax is more effective rely on internally generated correlations without independent demand or welfare validation.

The Maldives extension refits temperature and carbon functions and changes baseline terms, but does not publish local data files, diagnostics, constraints, optimizer settings, or an independent validation.
The Maldives resident-satisfaction equation changes denominators and coefficients without a complete mapping from Juneau variables, units, and weights.
The Maldives environmental damage equation assigns 0.3 temperature and 0.7 carbon weights without an AHP or decision-elicitation record.
The visual formula is 800x_1+200x_2+300x_3; any extracted 250x_2 reading is rejected, but the paper itself does not explain the attraction-price provenance.
The conclusion calls the model universal after one destination transfer, while the low-tourist policy section is qualitative and changes the priority logic.
Lower prices, publicity, welfare, and promotion are recommended without a demand model, destination capacity, budget, or spillover check.
Strengths claim scientific, reasonable, accurate, stable, and scalable behavior, but the paper does not provide the diagnostics needed for those strengths.
The self-evaluation does not acknowledge the index ambiguities, equation-number errors, units, missing-income simplification, optimizer settings, active-bound interpretation, or allocation conflicts.
The memo repeats model findings and recommends a roughly 1.43-million annual tourist level, but does not reconcile it with daily table values or the selected Pareto row.
Recommendations omit responsible owners, legal authority, monitoring fields, trigger thresholds, lags, failure conditions, equity analysis, and rollback rules.

Equations (21) and (22) split on prior revenue versus current cost but do not define equality handling, timing, caps, infeasible states, or a reproducible branch algorithm.
The ratio 6.5 is inferred from correlation coefficients rather than a cost-effectiveness or budget estimate; the correlation-to-cost mapping is unsupported.
The local perturbation heatmap is described as correlation strength, not a derivative or causal elasticity, and the perturbation grid and recalculation protocol are not published.
Claims that daily tourist limits dominate fixed fees or that hotel tax is more effective rely on internally generated correlations without independent demand or welfare validation.

The Maldives extension refits temperature and carbon functions and changes baseline terms, but does not publish local data files, diagnostics, constraints, optimizer settings, or an independent validation.
The Maldives resident-satisfaction equation changes denominators and coefficients without a complete mapping from Juneau variables, units, and weights.
The Maldives environmental damage equation assigns 0.3 temperature and 0.7 carbon weights without an AHP or decision-elicitation record.
The visual formula is 800x_1+200x_2+300x_3; any extracted 250x_2 reading is rejected, but the paper itself does not explain the attraction-price provenance.
The conclusion calls the model universal after one destination transfer, while the low-tourist policy section is qualitative and changes the priority logic.
Lower prices, publicity, welfare, and promotion are recommended without a demand model, destination capacity, budget, or spillover check.
Strengths claim scientific, reasonable, accurate, stable, and scalable behavior, but the paper does not provide the diagnostics needed for those strengths.
The self-evaluation does not acknowledge the index ambiguities, equation-number errors, units, missing-income simplification, optimizer settings, active-bound interpretation, or allocation conflicts.
The memo repeats model findings and recommends a roughly 1.43-million annual tourist level, but does not reconcile it with daily table values or the selected Pareto row.
Recommendations omit responsible owners, legal authority, monitoring fields, trigger thresholds, lags, failure conditions, equity analysis, and rollback rules.

writing_logic.summary: Summary: Juneau's wealth-pressure conflict, three models, objectives, NSGA-II, Pareto choice, expenditure feedback, sensitivity, Maldives transfer, and low-tourist use -> advance model by model in body order and show why each next model is needed -> compress task, mechanism, selected values, result-triggered switching, testing, and transfer -> a first-page decision ladder with an explicit model-I-to-II trigger -> Introduction.

Introduction: wilderness, cruise wealth, resident crowding, glacier retreat, TBMP limits, TSMP demand, official tasks, literature, and Our Work -> move from concrete conflict and a visible glacier change to failed existing management, task restatement, method selection, and workflow -> make multi-objective optimization and expenditure feedback feel earned rather than announced -> a bounded problem contract and workflow -> Assumptions.

Assumptions: market stability, tourist preferences, scenic allocation, hotel choice, and additional local premises -> pair each premise with a short empirical or tractability justification -> expose what is frozen before the optimization and elasticity equations -> a premise-consequence envelope -> Notation.

Notation: tourists, attractions, fees, hotel tax, road area, infrastructure, residents, waste, environment, and objectives -> freeze symbols in a compact ledger before data and formulas -> type the cross-model interface and preserve missing-unit boundaries -> a variable and unit interface -> Model Preparation.

Model Preparation: data needs, database sites, Juneau map, tourist scale, temperature, carbon, roads, capacity, prices, and waste -> say that the prompt does not directly provide the required data, then specify collection and visualization -> turn missing inputs into a source inventory and model handoff -> a prepared Juneau input ledger -> Multi-objective overview.

Multi-objective Overview: fiscal revenue, environmental damage, resident satisfaction, direct controls, and capacity constraints -> show the three objectives and their flow before local construction -> separate objective meanings, decisions, assumptions, and constraints -> a multi-objective architecture contract -> Fiscal Revenue.

Fiscal Revenue: three attraction counts and fees, hotel occupancy/spending, tax rate, and policy increases -> introduce attraction and hotel mechanisms locally before combining them -> construct fiscal revenue and hand tourist volume to environmental and demand models -> Equations (1)-(3) -> Environmental Damage.

Environmental Damage: visitor volume, temperature, carbon footprint, pandemic-year exclusion, historical extrema, and weights -> show both fitted functions, state an outlier decision, then normalize them into one objective -> connect data exclusion and fitted mechanisms to environmental damage -> Equations (4)-(6) -> Resident Satisfaction.

Resident Satisfaction: resident income, road congestion, infrastructure pressure, AHP weights, 2023 attitudes, road area, waste capacity, and population -> decompose positive and negative effects, assign weights, score the baseline, then write and simplify the objective -> construct a resident objective while preserving the missing-income and scale boundaries -> Equations (7)-(8) and a weighted satisfaction interface -> Constraints and demand.

Constraints and Demand Elasticity: attraction closure, tourist limits, fee and tax increases, income, prices, road area, alternative-city spending, and environmental thresholds -> move from a relaxed restriction to a binding equality, then use unavailable income to trigger a reduced demand specification -> close the feasible set and relate demand to policy controls -> Equations (9)-(18) -> NSGA-II.

NSGA-II and Pareto Selection: three objectives, feasible population, nondominated sorting, variation, 255 candidates, three distinct groups, and four similar solutions -> name the algorithm need, show its state changes, then visibly discard two groups before retaining the third -> turn a Pareto surface into a bounded set of policy candidates -> a candidate set and an explicit exclude-retain chain -> Expenditure feedback.

Expenditure Feedback: upper-bound road/capacity variables, additional tax/fee revenue, expenditure costs, satisfaction weights, and prior-year revenue -> let the selected result trigger a second model and split sufficient versus insufficient revenue -> translate optimization output into a time-lagged budget feedback interface -> Equations (19)-(22) and two expenditure branches -> Sensitivity.

Sensitivity: plus/minus ten-percent local perturbations, decision variables, three objectives, and a correlation heatmap -> state the perturbation protocol, read exact coefficient magnitudes, and turn them into factor-specific actions -> identify which controls the source treats as influential -> a heatmap-to-policy reading -> Maldives Expansion.

Maldives Expansion: Maldives attraction geography, tourists, emissions, temperature, prices, hotel occupancy, waste, residents, objectives, and result charts -> retain the model skeleton but remove or reweight locally inappropriate terms, refit functions, solve, and compare -> test structural transfer through explicit local changes rather than blind copying -> Equations (23)-(25), transferred Pareto results, and a Juneau comparison -> Low-tourist transfer.

Low-tourist Transfer: low visitor volume, price sensitivity, promotion, welfare, project development, and tourist diversion -> reverse Juneau's policy emphasis when the destination begins with too few tourists -> translate model relationships into lower-price, attraction, and promotion actions -> a qualitative low-tourism policy sketch -> Evaluation.

Evaluation: claimed comprehensiveness, quantification, practicality, stability, scalability, data limits, and proposed penalties -> separate four strengths from weaknesses and improvements -> bound the model's positive claims and retain its repair agenda -> a source-authored strengths/weaknesses ledger -> Memo.

Memo: council audience, selected tourist volume, fee/tax changes, road/capacity spending, implementation recommendations, limits, and monitoring -> open with the current burden, recap the model and values, list actions, then admit data/time limits -> translate the technical chain into an institutional recommendation -> a council-facing TSMP memo -> References boundary.
